title: Let's Encrypt has stopped issuing certificates for the shop
intro: After this morning's deploy, https://shop.example.com shows a certificate warning: it's serving the ingress controller's self-signed default. The Certificate shop-tls in namespace shop isn't Ready. The same pipeline has deployed to production several times a day for months without trouble. This week it was changed to 'start clean' by deleting and recreating the namespace's resources on each deploy.

steps.fake_output:
NAME       READY   SECRET     AGE
shop-tls   False   shop-tls   38m

steps.prompt: Not ready for 38 minutes. Follow the chain down: look at the orders in namespace shop.
The order errored. Find out why.
steps.fake_output:
Status:
  State:   errored
  Reason:  Failed to create Order: 429 urn:ietf:params:acme:error:rateLimited: Error creating new order :: too many certificates (5) already issued for this exact set of domains in the last 168 hours: shop.example.com, retry after 2026-09-30T06:14:00Z

steps.prompt: Rate limited: five certificates for exactly this name in the past week, and no more until 30 September. A certificate lasts 90 days, so something asked for five in a week. See what happened to the Secret that should hold it: list recent events in namespace shop mentioning shop-tls.
expected_commands: kubectl get events -n shop | grep shop-tls
kubectl get events -n shop --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep shop-tls
steps.fake_output:
38m   Normal   Issuing     certificate/shop-tls   Issuing certificate as Secret does not exist
38m   Normal   Generated   certificate/shop-tls   Stored new private key in temporary Secret resource "shop-tls-7kq2m"
38m   Warning  Failed      certificate/shop-tls   The certificate request has failed to complete and will be retried
steps.hint: kubectl get events -n shop | grep shop-tls

steps.prompt: 'Issuing certificate as Secret does not exist.' The new 'start clean' deploy deletes the Secret every time, so every deploy requests a brand-new certificate. Five deploys used up the week's allowance. You can't get a real certificate from Let's Encrypt until the 30th, but the company's internal-ca issuer isn't rate limited and the load balancer in front trusts it. Point the Certificate at it: patch shop-tls so spec.issuerRef.name is internal-ca.
expected_commands: kubectl patch certificate shop-tls -n shop --type merge -p '{"spec":{"issuerRef":{"name":"internal-ca"}}}'

steps.fake_output:
NAME       READY   SECRET     AGE
shop-tls   True    shop-tls   41m

resolution: Let's Encrypt allows five certificates per week for an identical set of names. A healthy setup uses one every sixty days, so the limit is normally invisible. This week's pipeline change made each deploy delete the namespace's resources, including the Secret holding the certificate and its private key. cert-manager, seeing a Certificate with no Secret, did its job and requested a new one. Five deploys later the allowance was gone, the sixth deploy deleted the last good certificate, and the request to replace it was refused until two days from now. The site was left on the ingress controller's self-signed default. Rate limits like this can't be lifted on request, which is what makes them dangerous: the fix has to come from elsewhere. Here the internal CA could stand in, because the load balancer in front of the cluster trusts it. Without that, the options are worse: a certificate for a different set of names (adding www counts as a different set), or another authority. The causes to remove are two. A deploy must never delete a certificate's Secret: treat it as state, like a database, not as something to recreate. Exclude it from 'clean' steps, or keep certificates in a namespace the pipeline doesn't touch. And anything that requests certificates in a loop should use the staging issuer, whose limits are generous and whose certificates are untrusted: pipelines, test environments, and preview deployments should never talk to production Let's Encrypt. Finally, alert on Certificate objects that aren't Ready and on days-to-expiry of what's actually served; either would have caught this at the first failed order instead of at a customer's browser warning.
